stories.title: llm 0.33
stories.paragraph: Simon Willison released version 0.33 of his command-line LLM tool, with the most significant change being an upgrade to the OpenAI Python library 3.x and a switch of the HTTP client dependency from httpx to httpx2. The release also expands embedding functionality, with llm embed and llm embed-multi now accepting a --key flag. A quick patch, version 0.32.1, had already been shipped the day before to address an immediate issue, with 0.33 serving as the more comprehensive resolution.

stories.title: Linus Torvalds Endures a Debug Session from Hell, "Enormously Helped" by AI
stories.paragraph: Linux creator Linus Torvalds described a difficult debugging session that he said was enormously helped by an AI assistant handling much of the routine investigative work. Notably, Torvalds also reported that the AI repeatedly declared the problem impossible and unsolvable and suggested simply writing a report, a tendency he attributed to training choices rather than technical limitation. The account illustrates both the practical utility and the persistence limitations of current AI coding assistants when applied to genuinely hard problems.

stories.title: Quoting Linus Torvalds
stories.paragraph: Simon Willison highlighted Torvalds's account of the same debugging session, quoting his observation that the AI acted as a tireless helper for grunt-work while still being willing to give up on problems Torvalds was not. Willison's framing draws attention to the tension between AI tools that accelerate routine tasks and their tendency to flag problems as unsolvable prematurely. The quote surfaces a recurring practitioner concern about AI assistants optimizing for appearing helpful rather than persisting through difficulty.

stories.title: More than just code review
stories.paragraph: Simon Willison argued that the core skill for working productively with coding agents is the ability to confidently instruct them and then verify their output, which does not always require reading every line of code they produce. He contends that line-by-line eyeballing has never been the most effective verification method, and that developers who can direct and audit agents at a higher level will be more effective than those who default to exhaustive manual review. The piece is framed as a practical reframing of what developer oversight looks like when working alongside automated coding tools.

stories.title: 80% of developers find AI coding more addictive than helpful
stories.paragraph: A survey reported by ZDNet found that 80 percent of developers described AI coding tools as more addictive than genuinely helpful, suggesting that the compulsive engagement these tools generate may be distinct from measurable productivity gains. The finding echoes concerns raised by Palantir CEO Alex Karp about AI products being designed to foster dependency rather than deliver value. The result points to a growing gap between developers' felt experience of using AI coding assistants and objective assessments of their impact on output quality or speed.

stories.title: Why can AI generate Super Mario but not a wedge ramp for my robot vacuum?
stories.paragraph: A Hacker News discussion explored the gap between AI image and creative generation capabilities and the current state of AI-driven 3D modeling for functional, physically constrained objects. The original poster, who owns a Bambu P2S 3D printer but cannot model, tried multiple text-to-3D tools to generate a simple wedge ramp for a robot vacuum step transition and found the output unusable. The thread highlights that while generative AI has advanced considerably for visual and textual media, producing geometrically precise, functionally valid CAD-style models remains a largely unsolved problem.

stories.title: Palantir's Karp – frontier AI labs that are 'trying to drug addict us'
stories.paragraph: Palantir CEO Alex Karp publicly accused frontier AI labs, referencing companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, of designing products intended to create dependency in users rather than deliver substantive utility. Karp's remarks, reported by CNBC, position Palantir as taking a distinct approach to AI deployment, focused on enterprise and government use cases rather than consumer engagement. The comments are notable given that Palantir is itself a significant AI software vendor, making the critique as much a competitive positioning statement as a policy concern.

stories.title: Anthropic IPO filing will show AI backlash as a risk factor, sources say
stories.paragraph: Sources told CNBC that Anthropic's forthcoming IPO filing will formally list public backlash against AI as a material risk factor, a disclosure that would make explicit what many in the industry have discussed informally. The inclusion reflects regulatory and reputational uncertainty that investors will need to weigh, and it arrives as trust in both AI systems and their makers is measurably declining according to recent surveys. Anthropic, which was valued at $61.5 billion in a 2025 funding round, would be among the first major frontier AI labs to go public.

stories.title: Digging the grave of my skills: Hollywood creatives training AI to do their jobs
stories.paragraph: The Guardian reported on Hollywood writers, artists, and other creative workers who have taken jobs providing training data for AI systems designed to automate roles similar to their own, driven by financial pressure following industry strikes and production slowdowns. The workers describe the work as a form of economic coercion, where declining incomes in their primary fields leave few alternatives even when the outcome may accelerate displacement. The piece adds a labor-market dimension to ongoing debates about generative AI in creative industries, illustrating that the pipeline from human creative labor to AI capability often runs directly through the affected workers themselves.

stories.title: AI has failed to win people's trust. Its makers? less trusted
stories.paragraph: A report covered by Euronews found that public trust in AI systems remains low, and that trust in the companies building those systems is even lower, suggesting that corporate reputation is a compounding factor in adoption hesitancy. The finding is consistent with Anthropic's decision to include AI backlash as a named risk in its IPO documentation. The data point matters for the industry because trust deficits can translate into regulatory pressure, reduced enterprise adoption, and slower consumer uptake regardless of the underlying technical capabilities of deployed systems.

stories.title: NanoGPT Speedrun Frontier
stories.paragraph: PrimeIntellect published a tracker of the NanoGPT speedrun frontier, a community benchmark focused on training a small GPT-style model to a target validation loss on Shakespeare text in the least wall-clock time possible. The speedrun has become a reference point for evaluating hardware efficiency, optimizer choices, and low-level training tricks, with successive record holders documenting their methods publicly. Because the task is small enough to be reproduced on consumer hardware, it functions as an accessible but meaningful proxy for training efficiency research.

stories.title: Contextual News Search APIs: A Deep Comparison for AI, RAG, and Research
stories.paragraph: A GitHub repository published a detailed side-by-side comparison of news search APIs evaluated specifically for use in AI pipelines, retrieval-augmented generation systems, and research applications. The comparison examines factors such as query flexibility, freshness of results, coverage, and cost, which are criteria that differ from general-purpose search benchmarks. As RAG architectures increasingly rely on real-time or recent news as context, the choice of underlying news retrieval API has become a practical engineering decision with measurable effects on output quality.

stories.title: Dutch regulator fines Uber €825M for letting AI deactivate driver accounts
stories.paragraph: The Dutch Data Protection Authority has fined Uber €825 million for allowing an automated algorithm to deactivate driver accounts without adequate human oversight or transparent explanation. The case is notable because it represents one of the largest fines levied against a company specifically for delegating consequential employment decisions to an automated system. Regulators found that affected drivers were not given sufficient information about how the algorithm reached its conclusions, violating EU data protection requirements around automated decision-making. The ruling sets a precedent for how gig-economy platforms may be required to handle AI-driven enforcement actions against workers.
